::: {.csf-hero}
<p class="csf-hero__eyebrow">Since March 2022</p>

<h1 class="csf-hero__title">It started because nobody had a <em>kitchen</em></h1>

<p class="csf-hero__lede">
Cuochi senza fuochi began in March 2022 between people who lived in the same few
streets in Padova, had never spoken to each other, and between them owned about one
working oven.
</p>
:::

::: {.csf-section}
<h2 class="csf-section__title">The problem we noticed</h2>

Arriving in a new city follows a script. You find a room you can afford. You work out
how to get to the university or the office. Both of those get solved in the first month,
because both of them have a market, a price and a contract.

Then the script runs out. There is no listing site for *people who live near you and
would also like some company*. Full time work or a full course load leaves almost no
room to go looking, and the standard options are worse than they sound: bars charge you
every time, clubs are too loud to talk in, and apps hand you back the same screen you
were trying to get away from.

So the format was kept as simple as it could possibly be. **One table, one recipe,
somebody's flat, no money changing hands, and nothing that needs to be switched on.**

::: {.csf-quote}
With a room and a commute, the capital is guaranteed. But what about **human capital**?
Is it easy to find new like minded people? Working full time makes it too hard.

<cite>the note that started the whole thing, March 2022</cite>
:::
:::

::: {.csf-section}
<h2 class="csf-section__title">Why cooks without fires</h2>

Because none of us had a real kitchen. Student rooms and shared flats come with two hobs
that half work, no oven, and a fridge shared between five people. That could have been
the reason not to do it. Instead it became the constraint that defined the whole thing:
if the recipe needs no fire, then everybody can take part, including the person who has
never made anything in their life.

It also settles the question of what to make. Desserts are the category where cooking
without heat stops being a compromise, so that is mostly what we do: things that get
crushed, whipped, layered and left in a fridge.

And it keeps the door genuinely open. The barrier to entry is turning up.
:::

::: {.csf-section}
<h2 class="csf-section__title">What it is, and what it isn't</h2>

::: {.csf-grid}
::: {.csf-card}
<span class="csf-card__icon"><i class="bi bi-people"></i></span>

### It is
A free, roughly monthly gathering in Padova where a group makes a dessert or an easy
recipe together without an oven, mostly for people who arrived recently for work or study.
:::

::: {.csf-card}
<span class="csf-card__icon"><i class="bi bi-fire"></i></span>

### It isn't
A potluck, a restaurant, a paid cooking class, a networking event, a dating app or a
business. Nobody is paid and nobody pays. You do not bring a dish.
:::

::: {.csf-card}
<span class="csf-card__icon"><i class="bi bi-heart"></i></span>

### What comes out of it
Neighbours. People do end up passing on flat leads, job tips and the name of a good
dentist, but that happens the way it happens between neighbours, not because it is the agenda.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.csf-section}
<h2 class="csf-section__title">Who runs it</h2>

A small rotating group of people who have been coming since the start. Whoever has the
space that month hosts and does the shopping; everybody else turns up. There is no
committee, and there is nothing to join beyond arriving.

If you have a flat with a big enough table and a fridge with room in it, tell us. That
is how the next few sessions get scheduled.
:::

::: {.csf-band}
